overview.text: Bernoulli’s principle describes how pressure, speed, and height trade off in moving fluids through conservation of mechanical energy. In the familiar level-flow case, when height is unchanged, faster-moving fluid has lower static pressure; the broader Bernoulli equation includes gravitational height as well. The idealized relation is used for incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline, so it is not a rule that can be applied without checking conditions. Named for Swiss mathematician and physicist Daniel Bernoulli, it appeared in his 1738 work Hydrodynamica. It helps explain devices such as pitot tubes, which infer fluid speed from pressure differences, but it should not be treated as a complete, stand-alone explanation of how airplane wings produce lift.

key_facts.text: Bernoulli’s equation expresses conservation of mechanical energy in a fluid: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume sum to a constant along a streamline under the stated ideal conditions.
For flow at constant height, the equation simplifies: if fluid speed increases, static pressure decreases, assuming the other conditions of the model hold.
The familiar form applies to incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline; real flows may require accounting for effects the idealized relation leaves out.
The principle is named after Daniel Bernoulli; OpenStax notes that he published studies of fluid motion in Hydrodynamica in 1738.
A pitot tube uses pressure differences to measure fluid speed; aircraft commonly use this type of device for air-speed indication.

Bernoulli’s equation can relate airflow speed to pressure around a wing, but NASA cautions that the “equal transit time” explanation of lift misapplies it; wing lift involves the overall flow and pressure around the body.
